Result: Introduction of InfraGraph for detailed infrastructure representation and a new GPU execution model, facilitating design space exploration in distributed ML.

Conclusion: The updated simulator enables exploration of optimized collective algorithms, network requirements, and GPU architectures.

Abstract: Distributed machine learning (ML) is a key paradigm for today's large-scale artificial intelligence applications. As model inference arises as an important use case, faithful modeling of latency-sensitive collective communication has never been more important. Capturing the device architecture and modeling control and data paths at high fidelity is therefore a necessity today. Having a common, detailed representation for distributed ML infrastructure is also crucial. We revisit the promising open-source, community-driven simulator: ASTRA-sim. In this work, we identify limitations of the current ASTRA-sim simulator and augment it with new features. To this end, we enable fine-grained, high-fidelity simulation with a standardized infrastructure representation, opening new design space exploration opportunities. We propose the simulation at cache-line-sized load-store granularity, with a detailed graphics processing unit (GPU) execution model, to balance simulation scalability and fidelity. We also introduce InfraGraph, a standardized representation to capture distributed ML network infrastructure in detail. Using the updated ASTRA-sim 3.0 simulator, we showcase interesting design space explorations for designing optimized collective algorithms, network requirements, and GPU architectures.

</details>


### [181] [Generalizing LCL Complexity Gaps to Unbounded Degree via Monadic Second-Order Properties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10693)
*Chiara Piombi*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: This paper generalizes Locally Checkable Labeling (LCL) problems to unbounded degree graphs using Local PMSO (LPMSO) problems. It extends classification and complexity observations from bounded degree graphs to unbounded degree rooted trees, proving existing complexity gaps are applicable to LPMSO problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the restrictions of LCL problems which are confined to bounded degree graphs, thereby enabling a broader understanding of complexity in local algorithms.

Method: Introduces Local PMSO (LPMSO) problems that are described by Presburger monadic second-order formulas and verified locally in constant time, extending traditional LCL results to unbounded degree graphs.

Result: Proves that complexity gaps observed in LCL problems also apply to LPMSO problems on unbounded degree rooted trees, retaining their decidability.

Conclusion: The findings indicate that the complexity classifications and gaps are not merely constraints of bounded degree graphs, thereby broadening the landscape of locally checkable problems.

Abstract: The last decade of research on the LOCAL model has seen tremendous progress in understanding locally checkable labeling (LCL) problems, culminating in an almost complete classification of the possible complexities LCL problems can exhibit. In particular, on undirected trees, Chang and Pettie showed that there is no LCL problem with complexity between $ω(\log n)$ and $n^{o(1)}$ and Chang showed that, for every positive integer $k$, there is no LCL problem with complexity between $ω(n^{1/(k+1)})$ and $o(n^{1/k})$; additionally, which side of each gap a problem is found on is decidable.
  While the class of LCL problems - which, roughly speaking, consists of problems for which the correctness of a solution can be described by a finite set of allowed node configurations, which in turn can be locally verified by a constant-time algorithm - includes many important problems, it has one major restriction: problems can be defined only on bounded degree graphs, which consequently restricts all the classification and gap results mentioned above.
  In this work, we propose a generalization of LCL problems to unbounded degree using Presburger monadic second-order (PMSO) formulas; more specifically, we consider what we call Local PMSO (LPMSO) problems, i.e., problems whose correct solutions are both finitely described by a PMSO formula and locally verifiable by a LOCAL algorithm in constant time - this class contains many of the important problems studied in the LOCAL model but defines them on unbounded degree graphs. As our main result we prove that, on unbounded degree rooted trees, the aforementioned $ω(\log n)$ - $n^{o(1)}$ and $ω(n^{1/(k+1)})$ - $o(n^{1/k})$ complexity gaps (and their decidability) extend to the class of LPMSO problems.

</details>


### [182] [Dynamic Software Updates using CRDTs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10920)
*Seppe Wyns,Jim Bauwens,Elisa Gonzalez Boix*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: The paper explores the application of Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) for dynamic software updates in distributed applications, proposing an App CRDT that manages application code and versions to facilitate updates without disrupting functionality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to enable seamless dynamic updates in distributed systems while ensuring compatibility with older versions and maintaining operational integrity.

Method: The authors propose the App CRDT model to manage application code linked to semantic versions, integrating with a message delivery middleware that supports partial updates.

Result: The proposed approach was implemented in AmbientTalk and LuAT, demonstrating that the use of CRDTs for code replication can be generalized across different programming languages.

Conclusion: The study concludes that leveraging CRDTs allows for effective management of dynamic updates in distributed applications, minimizing disruption during the update process.

Abstract: This paper investigates how Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) can be used for dynamic software updates of distributed applications. We propose to model application updates as a new App CRDT that stores the application code associated with a semantic version, which defines a total order of the code updates. The App CRDT works with an API-compatible message delivery middleware, which allows applications to continue working with partially updated components in the face of backwards-incompatible software updates. We implemented our approach in AmbientTalk, an ambient-oriented programming language designed for distributed systems. We show how this CRDT can be integrated with existing AmbientTalk applications, requiring minimal changes. We also implemented our approach in LuAT, an ambient-oriented programming framework for Lua. This shows that our approach of using CRDTs to replicate code can be generalised to other programming languages.

</details>


### [183] [FairWave : A Fairness-Aware Asynchronous DAG-BFT Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10982)
*Syariful Mujaddiq*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: FairWave is a dual-channel DAG BFT protocol that enhances fairness in reward distribution and Sybil resistance compared to existing approaches while maintaining strong performance metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address shortcomings in existing DAG-BFT systems related to fairness and centralization in PoS mechanisms, particularly focusing on balancing Sybil resistance and equitable reward distribution.

Method: FairWave separates selection and reward distribution into dual channels, employing super-linear stake selection and sub-linear reward distribution, and uses a lagged reputation system.

Result: FairWave demonstrates superior fairness metrics (e.g., Gini coefficient of 0.149), robust empirical performance across extensive simulations, and maintains safety with strong theoretical underpinnings.

Conclusion: FairWave effectively mitigates centralization and inequities in reward distribution in BFT systems, showing significant improvements over traditional systems in both empirical and theoretical contexts.

Abstract: Combining asynchronous Byzantine Fault Tolerant (BFT) consensus with Proof-of-Stake (PoS) creates a trilemma between Sybil resistance, reward distribution fairness, and protection against persistent plutocracy. Existing DAG-BFT approaches (Narwhal+Tusk, Bullshark, and Mysticeti) prioritize liveness over the fairness implications of stake-based selection, resulting in persistent longitudinal centralization.FairWave is a dual-channel DAG BFT protocol that separates anchor selection from reward distribution. The selection channel is super-linear in stake, guaranteeing Sybil gain < 1 for all split factors K > 1. The reward channel is sub-linear, using square-root stake normalization to mitigate rich-get-richer dynamics.The finalized DAG structure provides deterministic uptime and latency factors, allowing honest validators to agree on operational quality without any external oracle. To avoid circular dependency between selection outcomes and selection weights, reputation is used in a lagged form: the active value at epoch e equals the prior epoch's final value. We derive closed-form constraints for both channels and validate them through nine empirical analyses (approximately 550,000 Monte Carlo rounds) against eight baselines. FairWave achieves a Gini coefficient of 0.149 (vs. Pure-PoS's 0.488), a monotone HHI reduction from 0.039 to 0.021 over 50,000 epochs, an optimal-adversary Sybil split of K* = 1, and a success-rate coefficient of variation of 5.2% under +/-25% input perturbation. Safety (agreement and validity) is a formal consequence of the 2f+1 strong-support commit rule, holding unconditionally for f < n/3; the empirical differential is the monotone-continuous liveness-degradation curve, which decreases from 99.6% commit rate at b=0.20 to 71.1% at the theoretical bound b=1/3 without the discontinuous cliff characteristic of view-change-driven leader-BFT.

</details>


### [184] [A Neurosymbolic Prolog Skill for LLM-Driven Service Placement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11113)
*Jacopo Massa,Giuseppe Bisicchia,Patrizio Dazzi,Antonio Brogi*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: The paper proposes a neuro-symbolic approach for service placement in cloud-edge continuum, facilitating transparent and constraint-aware deployment of application components.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limitations of existing optimization models and neural methods in service placement that either lack transparency or formal guarantees.

Method: Utilizes a Prolog skill as an interface for generating and querying schema-constrained facts, allowing high-level intent to be structured into symbolic rules while using Prolog for validation and reasoning.

Result: Provides a framework that bridges high-level intent with formal constraint evaluation, enabling more inspectable and policy-aware placement decisions.

Conclusion: The neuro-symbolic approach enhances the service placement process by combining the strengths of symbolic reasoning with the capabilities of neural methods.

Abstract: Service placement in the cloud-edge continuum requires assigning application components to heterogeneous resources under multiple constraints, including latency, locality, and policy requirements. Existing approaches rely on optimisation models or heuristics that require explicit modelling, while neural methods lack transparency and formal guarantees. This work proposes a neuro-symbolic alternative based on a Prolog skill, a reusable interface for schema-constrained fact generation and querying, for constraint-aware placement. The skill enables a language model to structure placement intent into symbolic facts, rules, and queries, while delegating validation and reasoning to Prolog. This design bridges high-level intent and formal constraint evaluation, enabling inspectable and policy-aware placement decisions in cloud-edge environments.

</details>


### [185] [Revisiting "Cooler is Better": ITD-Aware Per-CPU Thermal Optimization for Sustainable Data Center Operation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11163)
*Jason Crop,Hayden Moore,Sudeep Pasricha*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Optimizing CPU temperatures in data centers can boost energy efficiency and sustainability, as modern low-voltage CPUs exhibit non-monotonic performance related to temperature.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the energy demand constraints in data centers and challenge the assumption that cooler CPUs are always more efficient.

Method: Empirical characterization of inverse temperature dependence (ITD) on Intel Xeon CPUs and analysis of measurements from commercial cloud data centers.

Result: Findings reveal that many CPUs operate significantly below their efficiency-optimal temperatures, leading to energy waste.

Conclusion: Implementing ITD-aware strategies can reduce data center energy consumption by 4-13%, enhancing sustainability without compromising performance.

Abstract: As data center energy demand approaches grid-level constraints, optimizing conventional server infrastructure is essential for sustainable growth. The long-standing assumption that "cooler is better", i.e., lower CPU temperatures reduce power, does not fully hold for modern low-voltage CPUs, where inverse temperature dependence (ITD) drives higher supply voltages at lower temperatures. This creates a non-monotonic performance-per-watt curve where efficiency peaks at an intermediate thermal point. In this paper, for the first time, we empirically characterize ITD on production Intel Xeon CPUs and demonstrate that efficiency-optimal temperatures are CPU part-specific, and frequently higher than typical data center operating conditions. Measurements from commercial cloud data center platforms (Amazon, Equinix) reveal that approximately half of modern high-power CPUs operate about 10°C below their efficiency-optimal thermal point. By implementing ITD-aware thermal grouping of CPUs and inlet temperature adjustments, data center operators can optimize facility-level cooling and overall sustainability. Our case study shows that this approach can reduce total data center energy by 4-13% without sacrificing performance or reliability.

</details>


### [186] [Piper: A Programmable Distributed Training System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11169)
*Megan Frisella,Shubham Tiwari,Andy Ruan,Yi Pan,Parker Gustafson,Mat Jacob,Gilbert Bernstein,Stephanie Wang*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Piper is a distributed training system designed to simplify and enhance the adaptability of parallelism strategies in large-scale model training by decoupling strategy declaration from runtime implementation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The increasing complexity in large-scale model training necessitates flexible systems that can adapt to evolving parallelism strategies without manual intervention.

Method: Piper utilizes user-defined annotations and scheduling directives to transform a unified global training DAG (intermediate representation), allowing for strategy-agnostic execution plans to be compiled and run.

Result: Piper maintains performance parity with existing strategies like ZeRO while offering improved performance and memory efficiency with advanced scheduling capabilities in more complex parallelism configurations.

Conclusion: Piper successfully enhances the flexibility and efficiency of distributed training by enabling users to easily implement and adapt sophisticated parallelism strategies.

Abstract: Large-scale model training increasingly relies on composing multiple parallelism strategies, such as data, pipeline, and expert parallelism, together with memory-saving optimizations like ZeRO. Deployed systems for foundation model pretraining often rely on human experts to manually design a high-level parallelism strategy then implement the corresponding low-level execution strategy, making it difficult to adapt the system to new strategies. Meanwhile, many general-purpose frameworks are more flexible but their implementations are still tied to a fixed set of common parallelism strategies, making it challenging to integrate state-of-the-art strategies.
  We present Piper, a user-controllable distributed training system that decouples the strategy from the runtime implementation. Piper allows users to declare a comprehensive distributed training strategy with a small set of model annotations and scheduling directives. Each directive applies a transformation on Piper's intermediate representation (IR), a unified global training DAG that represents all computation and communication. Using this IR, Piper compiles per-device execution plans and executes them with a distributed runtime agnostic to the strategy. We show that the combined system maintains performance parity on commonly available strategies such as ZeRO, while also enabling additional performance and memory efficiency gains through joint scheduling of compute and communication in composed parallelism strategies such as DeepSeek-V3's DualPipe.

</details>


<div id='cs.RO'></div>

# cs.RO [[Back]](#toc)

### [187] [Uncertainty-Aware Motion Planning for Autonomous Driving in Mixed Traffic Environment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09958)
*Ming Cheng,Hao Chen,Ziyi Yang,Ziluowen Luo,Senzhang Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: The paper presents Uncertainty-Aware Motion Planning (UAMP) for autonomous vehicles to safely navigate mixed-traffic environments by incorporating uncertainty in human driver intent predictions into decision-making.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enhance the safety of autonomous vehicles in mixed traffic by accounting for the inherent uncertainty in human driving behavior.

Method: UAMP employs a proximity-aware uncertainty estimator to gauge human intent uncertainty and utilizes Uncertainty-Calibrated Value Learning (UCVL) to adjust for biases in value function learning.

Result: UAMP demonstrates improved safety and comfort in driving, alongside maintaining traffic efficiency, in various mixed-traffic scenarios compared to existing methods.

Conclusion: The proposed method effectively mitigates risks associated with ambiguous human behavior, marking an advancement in motion planning for autonomous vehicles.

Abstract: In mixed-traffic environments where autonomous and human-driven vehicles may co-exist, motion planning for autonomous vehicles requires anticipating the future behaviors of surrounding human drivers. Existing reinforcement learning-based methods generally directly incorporate the predicted human intents into the observation to enable a proactive planning. However, human intent is inherently uncertain due to the behavioral diversity, perception noise, and partial observability. Treating predicted intends as deterministic states can result in unsafe decisions for autonomous vehicles. To address this problem, we propose Uncertainty-Aware Motion Planning (UAMP), which incorporates uncertainty in human intent prediction for AV decision-making. Specifically, UAMP first introduces a proximity-aware uncertainty estimator to quantify the interaction-conditioned intent uncertainty and constructs an uncertainty-guided joint intent distribution over surrounding human-driven vehicles. Within this uncertainty set, UAMP further introduces Uncertainty-Calibrated Value Learning (UCVL) to correct value function learning biases arising from directly incorporating uncertain human intent predictions into the observation. Extensive experiments in various mixed-traffic scenarios show that UAMP significantly improves safety and driving comfort, while maintaining traffic efficiency compared with existing approaches. The code is released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/UAMP-5638.

</details>


### [188] [GHOST: Hierarchical Sub-Goal Policies for Generalizing Robot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10025)
*Sriram Krishna,Ben Eisner,Haotian Zhan,Ying Yuan,Haoyu Zhen,Chuang Gan,Shubham Tulsiani,David Held*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: GHOST is a framework that enhances the generalization of visuomotor manipulation policies through a hierarchical approach with distinct high-level and low-level policies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for visuomotor manipulation policies that can adapt beyond specific training scenarios.

Method: GHOST employs a high-level policy for predicting sub-goals in 3D space and a low-level controller that acts based on these goals, using end-effector heatmaps projected from multi-view RGB-D data.

Result: This framework consistently outperforms previous methods in terms of performance and robustness across various manipulation tasks and allows for easy integration of human demonstrations.

Conclusion: The hierarchical structure of GHOST enables efficient adaptation to new objects and tasks with minimal human input, facilitating the creation of robust manipulation policies.

Abstract: We present GHOST, a framework for learning visuomotor manipulation policies that generalize beyond the training distribution. GHOST factorizes control into (i) a high-level policy that predicts the next sub-goal as a distribution over 3D end-effector poses from multi-view RGB-D observations, and (ii) a low-level goal-conditioned controller that executes embodiment-specific actions. To condition image-based policies on 3D goals, we introduce a simple spatial interface that projects predicted goals into the image plane and represents them as end-effector heatmaps. Across a suite of manipulation tasks, this hierarchical factorization consistently improves performance and robustness compared to a flat Diffusion Policy.
  Further, we show that this hierarchical interface also makes it easy to incorporate human demonstrations without relying on (noisy) action retargeting. As sub-goals are largely embodiment-agnostic, we train the high-level policy on human video to specify how learned skills should be applied and composed, while keeping the low-level policy trained purely on robot data. This hierarchy enables adaptation to novel objects and task variations using a small number of human demonstrations.

</details>


### [189] [A Spiking Neural Architecture for Coordinating Arm and Locomotor Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11034)
*Lea Steffen,Kathryn Simone,Graeme Damberger,Travis DeWolf,Hudson Ly,Chris Eliasmith*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: This paper presents an integrated spiking controller for humanoid robot control, combining bipedal locomotion and arm control for energy efficiency using spiking neural networks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation behind this research is to advance humanoid robot control by integrating previously isolated motor control systems for better energy efficiency and capability in dynamic environments.

Method: The proposed method uses a spiking neural architecture integrating force-based arm and bipedal control, employing the Neural Engineering Framework (NEF) and Semantic Pointer Architecture (SPA), with action selection managed by a spiking basal ganglia model.

Result: The system was validated through co-simulation of Nengo and Isaac Sim, demonstrating successful performance in tasks such as target reaching, continuous digit drawing, and path-following locomotion, with effective switching between locomotion and arm control.

Conclusion: This work represents a significant step in humanoid control systems, showcasing the first spiking architecture to effectively integrate arm and bipedal movement in a humanoid robot, paving the way for low-power neuromorphic hardware implementation.

Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) coupled with neuromorphic hardware offer energy-efficient solutions for humanoid robot control. However, existing SNN-based motor control systems address bipedal locomotion and arm control in isolation, leaving integrated control of both unaddressed. We present a spiking architecture that coordinates force-based arm control and bipedal locomotion in a simulated humanoid, using the Neural Engineering Framework (NEF) and Semantic Pointer Architecture (SPA). High-level action selection between locomotor and arm control is mediated by a biologically grounded spiking basal ganglia model. We validate the system through co-simulation of Nengo, for the neural control, and Isaac Sim, demonstrating successful target reaching, continuous digit drawing, path-following locomotion, and finally, switching between walking and arm control via basal ganglia disinhibition. To our knowledge, this is the first integrated spiking controller to combine bipedal locomotion and arm control on a full-scale humanoid platform. The full spike-based implementation enables future deployment on low-power neuromorphic hardware.

</details>


### [190] [Robotic Nonprehensile Object Transportation with a Hanging Tray](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10039)
*Adam Heins,Angela P. Schoellig*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: This paper presents a novel approach to the waiter's problem by using a hanging tray suspended from the robot's end effector. This method reduces object sliding and liquid sloshing compared to a rigidly held tray while requiring a simpler actuator setup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The study aims to improve the transportation of objects by robots, particularly addressing the limitations of previous methods that required complex actuation for pendular motion.

Method: The researchers employed a hanging tray connected to a three-degree-of-freedom mobile base, allowing for pendular motion that minimizes shear forces while maintaining simplicity in robotic design.

Result: Experiments demonstrated that the hanging tray significantly reduces sliding of rigid objects and sloshing of liquid compared to traditional methods that use static trays.

Conclusion: Integrating the hanging tray with interactive capabilities enhances the robot's functionality as a waiter, showcasing improvements in object transport and interaction through computer vision and visual servoing.

Abstract: We consider the nonprehensile object transportation task known as the waiter's problem, in which a robot must move an object balanced on a tray from one location to another. In contrast to prior works on the robotic waiter's problem, which make the robot tilt a tray rigidly held by its end effector (EE), we use a tray suspended from the EE by ropes, such that it behaves like a three-dimensional pendulum. Some prior works have actuated the robot so that the EE simulates the behavior of a pendulum, because pendular motion reduces the shear forces acting on the transported objects, minimizing the sliding of rigid objects and sloshing in containers of liquid. In contrast, our use of a real hanging tray allows us to obtain the benefits of pendular motion while only actuating a 3 degree-of-freedom (DOF) mobile base, rather than requiring a full 6-DOF manipulator arm. Our experiments in simulation and on real hardware show that the hanging tray substantially reduces both sliding and sloshing compared to a static, rigidly-grasped tray. Furthermore, we integrate the hanging tray into an interactive robot waiter demonstration, which uses computer vision to identify people with a raised hand and visual servoing to steer toward them and allow them to access the tray.

</details>


### [191] [Efficient-WAM: A 1B-Parameter World-Action Model with Low-Cost Future Imagination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10040)
*Jiajun Li,Tiecheng Guo,Yifan Ye,Rongyu Zhang,Xiaowei Chi,Qianpu Sun,Ying Li,Yunfan Lou,Yan Huang,Zhihe Lu,Meng Guo,Shanghang Zhang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Efficient-WAM improves the efficiency of World-Action Models for embodied control by reducing inference costs while maintaining effective action generation, achieving a significant speedup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for a more efficient World-Action Model that enables real-time robot deployment by lowering inference latency associated with photorealistic future predictions.

Method: Efficient-WAM employs a compact video expert, token-sparse video latents, and asymmetric video-action denoising to optimize inference efficiency, treating future video prediction as guidance for action generation rather than focusing on visual fidelity.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that Efficient-WAM maintains strong action performance even with lower-quality future predictions, reducing per-chunk latency to around 100 ms and achieving a 30x speedup over traditional WAMs.

Conclusion: Efficient-WAM effectively balances the benefits of visual prediction with the need for faster inference, making it suitable for real-time robotic applications.

Abstract: World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied control by coupling future visual prediction with action generation. However, most existing WAMs rely on photorealistic future prediction, which incurs high inference latency and makes real-time robot deployment difficult. This motivates a more efficient WAM design that preserves the control benefits of future visual prediction while reducing its inference cost. We introduce Efficient-WAM, a World-Action Model that reduces the cost of future imagination while preserving its control benefit. Efficient-WAM improves inference efficiency via a compact video expert transferred from WAN-2.2-5B, token-sparse video latents, and asymmetric video-action denoising that allocates fewer sampling steps to video than to actions. Instead of optimizing the future branch for visual fidelity, Efficient-WAM treats future video prediction as a compact guidance signal for action generation. Comprehensive experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 and real-world manipulation tasks show that Efficient-WAM maintains strong action performance despite visibly coarse future predictions. While maintaining competitive control capabilities, our 1B-parameter model can reduce per-chunk latency to around 100 ms during physical deployment, achieving a 30x speedup over existing WAMs.

</details>


### [192] [Flow Control: Steering Vision-Language-Action Models with Simple Real-Time Inputs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10180)
*Jonathan C. Kao,Jason Chan,Andy Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Flow control enhances vision-language-action models' responsiveness to user inputs, improving task performance without the need for retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide a method for real-time steering of VLA actions based on user inputs, enhancing usability and performance in robotic tasks.

Method: Flow control uses generic inputs, such as keyboard commands, to guide VLA actions, drawing on learned expert action distributions for quality and fidelity.

Result: Flow control allows users to steer VLA actions accurately and robustly, achieving higher success rates and faster task completion, while also enabling improvements through fine-tuning.

Conclusion: Flow control offers a simple, effective approach for engaging users in the operation of VLA systems, significantly boosting performance.

Abstract: We introduce flow control of vision-language-action (VLA) models, a simple and effective way to steer VLA actions in real-time through generic inputs, such as a keyboard. This method can be used out-of-the-box and does not require retraining or fine-tuning VLAs. It enables relatively crude user inputs to steer a VLA to align with user intent. The VLA transforms these inputs into action samples drawn from the VLA expert action distribution learned during training, so that the generated actions are high quality (conformity to the action expert distribution) and high fidelity (reflecting the user's intent). We demonstrate that flow control has many desirable properties: (1) flow control accurately and responsively steers robot actions with user inputs, (2) it is robust to suboptimal user inputs, (3) it enables users to steer VLAs to achieve significantly higher success rates and faster task completion, and (4) fine-tuning a VLA on flow control trajectories improves the autonomous policy. Together, these results provide a simple and intuitive way for users to help steer VLA actions, increasing task performance.

</details>


### [193] [RocketSmith: An Agentic System for High-Powered Rocket Design and Manufacturing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00097)
*Peter Pak,Jesse Barkley,Rumi Loghmani,Derek Baich,Ananya Pamal,Amir Barati Farimani*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: RocketSmith is an automated system for designing, manufacturing, and optimizing high power rockets, which successfully created and tested various rocket configurations with high accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enhance the process of high powered rocket development through intelligent automation and optimization.

Method: An agentic system utilizing subagents and skills to automate design and manufacturing processes, conducting both zero-shot and human-in-the-loop optimization workflows.

Result: Four high power rockets with different configurations were designed and tested; all achieved stable launches with two successfully recovered, and 84% simulation accuracy for measured apogee.

Conclusion: RocketSmith demonstrates significant advancements in the automation of rocket development, resulting in successful rocket launches and high accuracy in flight predictions.

Abstract: This work presents RocketSmith, an agentic system capable of the design, manufacturing, and optimization processes in high powered rocket development. The system enables the intelligent automation of software tools as to not only validate factors such as flight stability but also generate the parametric design components for the rocket assembly. A collection of subagents and skills enable optimization workflows of flight parameters via iteration in both zero-shot and human-in-the-loop workflows. With this system, four distinct high power rockets with various motor and assembly configurations were developed utilizing the unique design capabilities of additive manufacturing. These assembly components were fabricated using various FDM printers, manually evaluated for flight readiness, and flight tested at a launch event. From these tests, all rockets achieved a stable launched and two of the four rockets were successfully recovered in reflyable condition. Within the collected flight data, an 84% accuracy was achieved when comparing measured apogee to that calculated in flight simulations.

</details>


### [194] [Exploration of Foundation Model-Based Robots in Patient and Elderly Care](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10208)
*Zhiwen Qiu,Wei Liu,Yuexing Hao*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: The paper discusses the integration of foundation models in care robots for older adults, highlighting their promise, current limitations, and areas for improved evaluation in clinical settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a growing demand for enhanced care for older adults, necessitating reliable and flexible technologies that can improve patient care and communication.

Method: The Perspective synthesizes existing foundation model-based care robots, focusing on design features, user experience, and outcomes related to care efficacy.

Result: While current systems show positive usability and engagement, they also exhibit significant reliability issues and primarily yield positive results in cognitive engagement without robust clinical impact evidence.

Conclusion: Future research should focus on developing care-specific evaluation standards and integrating these technologies into existing care workflows to enhance effectiveness and accountability.

Abstract: Demand for older-adult and patient care is growing rapidly as populations age worldwide. Foundation models are increasingly being integrated into robots and interactive agents, with the promise of more flexible communication and personalized assistance. However, care settings require reliable and workflow-compatible systems with accountable human oversight, and it remains unclear whether current embodied systems can translate technical advances into clinical impact. This Perspective synthesizes foundation model-based care robots across three areas: design features, user experience, and evidence for care-related outcomes. Current systems most commonly use foundation models as conversational and reasoning layers within voice-centered socially assistive embodiments, while multimodal grounding and physical autonomy remain limited. Empirical evaluations report positive usability and engagement benefits, but reliability failures persist across the interaction pipeline such as hallucinations and conversational breakdowns. Evidence for care impact remains concentrated in proximal outcomes such as cognitive engagement and participation, with limited evidence for validated clinical or care-related changes. We argue that future research should transition toward care-specific evaluation standards, accountable autonomy, and integration into care workflows to support more responsive and responsible care technologies.

</details>


### [195] [What Demonstration Curation Metrics Do to Your Policy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10229)
*Aarav Bedi*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Demonstration-curation metrics do not correlate with the performance of behavior-cloning policies trained on curated data. Results reveal that effective defect detection does not necessarily equate to improved policy outcomes, stressing the need for careful evaluation criteria.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the relationship between defect detection metrics and the effectiveness of behavior-cloning policies trained on curated datasets.

Method: Evaluated seven demonstration-curation metrics on a LIBERO pick-and-place benchmark with a controlled structural defect and analyzed their effect on the performance of behavior-cloning policies.

Result: The highest defect-detection AUROC metric led to the poorest performing policy, while a lower AUROC metric yielded a policy almost as effective as one trained on clean data, revealing a disconnection between defect detection and policy performance.

Conclusion: Curation methods should be assessed based on the resultant policy performance rather than merely defect detection rates, and the influence of episode length must be controlled in evaluations.

Abstract: We study whether demonstration-curation metrics that detect defective training episodes also improve the downstream behavior-cloning policy that trains on the curated data. On a contact-rich LIBERO pick-and-place benchmark with a controlled structural defect (early gripper release during the carry phase), we find that the two quantities are sharply decoupled. The metric with the highest defect-detection AUROC (0.804) produces the worst curated policy (13.3% task success), while a metric with a substantially lower AUROC (0.638) produces a policy that nearly matches the oracle trained on ground-truth clean data (90.0% vs. 93.3%). We further show that five of the seven metrics we evaluate exploit episode length as a trivial proxy for the defect label, a confound that inflates reported AUROCs to near-perfect values and disappears once episode length is controlled. Across all conditions, the contaminated baseline succeeds on only 3.3% of rollouts, and the two best curation methods close this to within 3 percentage points of the 93.3% oracle ceiling. Our results argue that curation methods should be evaluated by the policy they produce, not the defects they flag, and that any curation benchmark must control for episode length before reporting detection accuracy. We release the testbed, all metric implementations, and the evaluation pipeline.

</details>


### [196] [YUBI: Yielding Universal Bidigital Interface for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10244)
*Takehiko Ohkawa,Jumpei Arima,Yuki Noguchi,Masatoshi Tateno,Makoto Sugiura,Takuya Okubo,Kengo Ikeuchi,Yuma Shin,Hiroki Nishizawa,Naoaki Kanazawa,Yuki Wakayama,Daiki Fukunaga,Koshi Makihara,Tomohiro Motoda,Floris Erich,Yukiyasu Domae,Tatsuya Matsushima,Yohishiro Okumatsu,Kei Ota*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: The paper presents YUBI, a finger-aligned gripper for improved ergonomic data collection in bimanual dexterous manipulation, addressing limitations of existing handheld systems. It showcases a large-scale dataset and demonstrates advantages in versatility and efficiency across various robotic platforms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the ergonomic challenges and limitations of existing handheld data collection systems for fine-grained bimanual tasks, YUBI aims to provide a more intuitive and scalable solution.

Method: YUBI employs a finger-driven actuation mechanism that translates human finger movements to gripper jaw motion, complemented by a VR-based 6 DoF tracking system for precise data collection. A comprehensive dataset was compiled using this system.

Result: YUBI was tested against the existing UMI gripper, demonstrating superior versatility for complex tasks, improved dexterity, and operational efficiency. The dataset includes over 8,434 hours of data across diverse tasks.

Conclusion: The study highlights YUBI's effectiveness in facilitating robotic policy training across different platforms, with the release of hardware and datasets supporting reproducibility and advancement in robotic models.

Abstract: We introduce Yielding Universal Bidigital Interface (YUBI), a finger-aligned gripper designed to enable intuitive, ergonomic, and scalable data collection for bimanual dexterous manipulation. While handheld data collection systems such as Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) enable affordable data collection, their bulky pistol-grip designs can pose ergonomic and usability challenges for fine-grained, dexterous manipulation tasks. To address this, YUBI presents a distinct design principle: yielding, finger-driven actuation that directly maps human finger movements to gripper jaw motion. Using the YUBI devices, we set up a data collection system with integrated VR-based 6 DoF tracking of the gripper, ensuring high-fidelity trajectory data acquisition. We curate a UMI-based dataset of unprecedented scale: 8,434 hours across 1.20M episodes and 119 tasks. Experiments show that YUBI offers advantages over the UMI gripper in versatility for complex bimanual tasks, dexterity, and operational efficiency. A single policy trained on the YUBI dataset transfers across multiple bimanual robots (UR, Franka, and ELEY) simply by mounting the gripper on each platform, confirming that the collected data are directly executable as policy supervision. We release the gripper hardware, data-collection software, and dataset as one integrated stack, offering the open community a reproducible path to large-scale data acquisition for advancing robotic foundation models.

</details>


### [197] [What Matters in Orchestrating Robot Policies: A Systematic Study of Hierarchical VLA Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10267)
*Jiaheng Hu,Mohit Shridhar,Caden Lu,Dhruv Shah,Hao-Tien Lewis Chiang,Jie Tan,Annie Xie*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: This paper presents a systematic study of Hierarchical Vision-Language-Action (Hi-VLA) systems for robot manipulation, establishing unified design principles that enhance performance and robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the lack of unified design principles in existing Hi-VLA systems, which vary in planners, controllers, and task execution methodologies.

Method: A systematic exploration of Hi-VLA design under an options-style control framework, benchmarking design choices across various tasks including short-horizon, long-horizon, and reasoning-intensive scenarios.

Result: The analysis reveals practical principles for constructing Hi-VLA systems, resulting in a significantly stronger system compared to flat VLA control or naively designed hierarchies, validated through simulations and real-world experiments with the ALOHA robot.

Conclusion: The findings contribute to the foundation for developing more capable, robust, and coherent hierarchical VLA agents in robotic manipulation tasks.

Abstract: Hierarchical vision-language-action (Hi-VLA) systems have emerged as a promising paradigm for complex robot manipulation, by using high-level VLM planners to decompose tasks into language subgoals executed by low-level VLA controllers. Despite recent empirical progress, there is a lack of unified design principles for these systems: existing Hi-VLA systems differ in how they choose and connect planners, controllers, mechanisms to switch between the two, and how observations and memory are represented in the planner. In this paper, we present a systematic study of Hi-VLA design for robot manipulation. We unify representative Hi-VLA agents under an options-style control framework and benchmark core design choices across short-horizon, long-horizon, and reasoning-intensive tasks. Our analysis distills practical principles for building Hi-VLA systems, showing how model choices and interface mechanisms jointly shape performance. Applying these principles yields a substantially stronger system than either flat VLA control or a naively designed hierarchy, across experiments both in simulation and on a real ALOHA robot. Overall, our results provide a foundation for building more capable, robust, and principled hierarchical VLA agents. More information and video at jiahenghu.github.io/hi-vla.

</details>


### [198] [Locomotion analysis of a quadruped interacting with the lunar granular surface](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10273)
*Yash J Vyas*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: This study examines the challenges of legged robots on lunar regolith, focusing on the need for simulations that consider soft contact interactions to improve locomotion performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve the design and performance of quadrupedal robots for lunar exploration, given the unique challenges posed by the lunar regolith.

Method: The study employed physical modeling of granular surfaces to simulate robot foot contacts in a reinforcement learning environment, comparing locomotion policies under rigid versus soft contact conditions.

Result: The analysis revealed that locomotion trained on soft surfaces resulted in different gait patterns and greater energy expenditure compared to training on rigid surfaces.

Conclusion: To effectively operate on the lunar surface, locomotion algorithms must account for soft contacts, as they significantly influence gait and energy requirements.

Abstract: Deploying legged robots in extra-terrestrial environments includes many challenges due to complex terrain interactions, energy, and thermal constraints. For effective mechanical design of a lunar exploration quadrupedal robot, careful consideration of motor torques, energy expenditure, and cost of transport is required. The lunar surface is composed of granular regolith, which impacts the locomotion of legged robots and their performance. Locomotion algorithms trained with rigid contact assumptions are also ineffective when applied to environments with soft contacts, such as granular surfaces, which can result in instability and poor tracking. In this report, the physical modelling of the granular lunar surface-robot foot contacts is applied to a simulation environment with locomotion trained using Reinforcement Learning. A comparison is conducted between the policy trained on rigid contact and soft contact environments, analysing the gait and locomotion performance metrics. The analysis demonstrates that soft contacts simulating regolith surfaces pose additional challenges for Reinforcement Learning based training, result in a qualitatively different gait, and increase the overall energy expenditure.

</details>


### [199] [Hierarchical Policies from Verbal and Egocentric Human Signals for Natural Human-Robot Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10276)
*Dongjun Lee,Juheon Choi,Dong Kyu Shin,Sinjae Kang,Kimin Lee*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: EDITH is a robot framework that enhances natural human-robot interaction by combining verbal instructions with nonverbal signals from smart glasses, enabling effective understanding of human intent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve human-robot interaction by utilizing nonverbal signals (gestures and gaze) in conjunction with language instructions, addressing the limitations of current robot communication policies.

Method: EDITH captures continuous streams of first-person view and gaze data from smart glasses, processes this alongside transcribed speech to infer human intent using a hierarchical policy that breaks it into subtasks.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that EDITH allows robots to act on nonverbal signals, reducing user effort in conveying intent compared to using language alone.

Conclusion: By integrating nonverbal cues, EDITH significantly enhances the robot's responsiveness to human intent, facilitating more intuitive and efficient interactions.

Abstract: For natural human-robot interaction, a robot must understand human intent expressed not only through language but also through nonverbal signals such as gestures and gaze. However, current robot policies rely on language instructions as the sole interface for conveying intent, leaving nonverbal signals unused and placing the full burden of communication. In this work, we present EDITH, a robot framework that captures the human's nonverbal signals through continuous streams of first-person view and gaze from smart glasses, and uses them alongside language instructions as inputs to the robot policy. Our hardware system streams the human's first-person view, gaze, and speech to the robot in real time, transcribing the speech into language instructions. To handle these rich but noisy signals, we design a hierarchical policy in which a high-level policy infers the human's intent and produces a sequence of subtasks, where each subtask is represented as a fine-grained instruction paired with a keyframe that grounds the intent in the scene (e.g., the frame where the human points at the target object). A low-level policy then executes these subtasks. In our experiments on human-robot interactive tasks, EDITH enables the robot to act on the human's nonverbal signals even when intent is expressed only briefly, and significantly reduces user effort to convey intent compared to using language instructions alone. Visit our project page for source code and real-robot demo videos.

</details>


### [200] [MARCH: Model-Assisted Reinforcement Learning for the Perceptive Control of Humanoids over Sparse Footholds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10288)
*Codrin Crismariu,Ryan K. Cosner*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: This paper presents a model-assisted reinforcement learning framework for bipedal locomotion over sparse terrain, combining model-based and model-free methods to enhance safety and efficiency in robotic movement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the challenges of achieving precise and safe bipedal locomotion in environments with sparse footholds, while overcoming the limitations of both model-based and model-free methods.

Method: The proposed framework includes generating a safe reference trajectory with simplified models, training a privileged teacher policy using a control Lyapunov function, and distilling this teacher policy into a vision-based student policy.

Result: The model-assisted approach yields improved sample efficiency, smoother locomotion, and performance that matches model-free methods, validating its effectiveness in simulations and real-world scenarios with a humanoid robot.

Conclusion: The framework successfully combines the strengths of both modeling perspectives, allowing for safe and efficient navigation in challenging environments.

Abstract: Perceptive bipedal locomotion over sparse terrain remains a difficult challenge: model-based methods are precise but brittle to uncertainty, while model-free methods are robust but struggle to discover the precise, constrained motions required for safety-critical locomotion where small errors can cause catastrophic failures. We propose a model-assisted reinforcement learning (RL) framework that combines both perspectives in three steps: (1) generate a safe reference trajectory using simplified models; (2) train a privileged teacher policy guided by a control Lyapunov function (CLF) reward built around the safe reference trajectory; and (3) distill the teacher into a vision-based student policy. We show that this model-assistance procedure produces physically grounded locomotion, improving sample efficiency, reducing the need for a complex learning curriculum, and achieving smoother locomotion behavior alongside stepping stone performance comparable to model-free baselines. We validate our approach in simulation and demonstrate successful deployment on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot navigating sparse footholds with lateral constraints.

</details>


### [201] [Improved Representation of Matrix Lie Group Operations through Tensor Notation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10289)
*Clark Taylor*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: This paper presents a new mathematical notation for expressing operations with matrix Lie groups using tensors and Einstein summation, enhancing clarity in gradient-based estimation methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve accuracy and consistency in estimation problems involving Lie groups.

Method: Introduces tensors and Einstein summation notation for clearer representation of matrix Lie derivatives and operations.

Result: The new notation simplifies understanding and utilizing matrix Lie groups in estimation frameworks.

Conclusion: The paper emphasizes improved clarity in mathematical representation rather than introducing new capabilities.

Abstract: Several recent papers have demonstrated the utility of using Lie groups within estimation problems, yielding improved accuracy and consistency. This paper introduces a new tool for describing operations with matrix Lie groups: tensors and the Einstein summation notation. While tensors and Einstein notation are well-known in other research fields, applying this mathematical notation to represent and compute matrix Lie derivatives is novel. More importantly, this new notation greatly clarifies the derivatives and operations necessary to work with matrix Lie Groups in (gradient-based) estimation frameworks. Therefore, the main contribution of this paper is not a new capability, but a more perspicuous mathematical notation for working with matrix Lie groups.

</details>


### [202] [SARM2: Multi-Task Stage Aware Reward Modeling for Self Improving Robotic Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10305)
*Qianzhong Chen,Hau Zheng,Justin Yu,Suning Huang,Jiankai Sun,Ken Goldberg,Chuan Wen,Pieter Abbeel,Yide Shentu,Philipp Wu,Mac Schwager*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Introduction of a multi-task stage-aware reward model (RM) and a new framework (SPIRAL) to enhance vision-language-action policies for long-horizon manipulation with improved task success rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The dependence on behavior cloning for fine-tuning long-horizon VLA policies limits their effectiveness due to the need for high-quality demonstrations and constraining policies to the demonstration distribution.

Method: RM is a multi-task stage-aware reward model that employs a stage estimator with a multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts value head, producing dense rewards for tasks. SPIRAL leverages RM in an on-policy reward-guided framework for improving VLA policies via low-cost autonomous rollouts.

Result: RM achieves an 80% reduction in value-estimation MSE and when applied in SPIRAL, significantly improves task success rates (58% to 100% in Folding Shorts and 50% to 90% in Cleaning Whiteboard).

Conclusion: The research demonstrates that using high-quality dense rewards is crucial for enhancing robot learning and performance in manipulation tasks.

Abstract: Fine-tuning vision-language-action (VLA) policies for long-horizon manipulation still relies heavily on behavior cloning, which requires costly high-quality demonstrations and keeps policies near the demonstration distribution. Reward models can reduce this dependence by reweighting demonstrations and providing dense supervision for on-robot reinforcement learning (RL), but they must be dense, accurate, and general. Existing methods fall short: task-specific stage-aware models are accurate but require per-task annotations, while general vision-language-model (VLM) reward models are broadly applicable but too coarse for fine-grained long-horizon progress. We introduce RM, a multi-task stage-aware reward model that combines an action-primitive-based stage estimator with a multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts (MMoE) value head to produce dense per-step rewards across manipulation tasks. Building on RM, we further propose SPIRAL (Self-Policy Improvement via Reward-Aligned Learning), an on-policy reward-guided framework that improves VLA policies from cheap autonomous rollouts. On a 10-task benchmark, RM reduces value-estimation MSE by 80% over the strongest baselines; when used in SPIRAL, it improves task success from around 50% to near-perfect performance on Folding Shorts (58% to 100%) and Cleaning Whiteboard (50% to 90%), showing that high-quality dense rewards are key to a stable robot data flywheel. Project website: https://qianzhong-chen.github.io/sarm2.github.io/.

</details>


### [203] [OMG: Omni-Modal Motion Generation for Generalist Humanoid Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10340)
*Siqiao Huang,Kun-Ying Lee,Dongming Qiao,Guanqi He,Zhenyu Wang,Yitang Li,Shaoting Zhu,Hang Zhao*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: The paper presents OMG, a humanoid control approach that integrates a scalable module for diverse input modalities with a motion tracking system, overcoming limitations of existing methods through advanced data management and motion generation techniques.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To advance humanoid whole-body control beyond limited skill policies and challenging extensibility of current motion trackers, aiming for a general-purpose control system.

Method: OMG features a meticulous data curation, filtering, and labeling pipeline coupled with a diffusion-based motion generation backend that supports conditioning on various inputs, including language and audio.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that OMG functions as an omni-modal whole-body controller, achieving state-of-the-art performance and adaptability to new modalities and distributions.

Conclusion: OMG marks a significant advancement toward developing foundational models for humanoid robots.

Abstract: Humanoid whole-body control has made significant progress in recent years, yet existing approaches remain limited to few-skill policies with heavy reward engineering, or motion trackers that are difficult to extend to new input modalities. We argue that the key to general-purpose humanoid control is to build a scalable brain, a module capable of reasoning with diverse conditioning modalities, atop a reactive motion tracking cerebellum, mirroring the hierarchical structure of biological motor systems. Two challenges arise in realizing this vision: acquiring a vast amount of high-quality data to achieve general purpose control, and equipping the generator with the capability to condition on compositional, extensible multi-modal inputs. We present OMG, which addresses these challenges with a meticulous data curation, filtering and labeling pipeline, as well as a diffusion-based motion generation backbone that conditions on language, audio, and human reference motions. Extensive experiments validate OMG as an omni-modal whole-body controller exhibiting state-of-the-art performance, model scaling behavior and efficient adaptation to new distributions and modalities, marking a concrete step toward foundation models for humanoid robots.

</details>


### [204] [Rethinking Embodied Navigation via Relational Inductive Bias](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10348)
*Weitao An,Chenghao Xu,Xu Yang,Cheng Deng*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: DB-Nav improves object navigation by using dual relational biases to enhance search reliability while suppressing unreliable cues, outperforming existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing navigation methods neglect the unreliability of certain semantic cues, which can mislead the agent's search and decision-making processes.

Method: DB-Nav utilizes Activation and Inhibition Biases to reshape the search space, incorporating a Relational Activation-Inhibition Exploration Graph to guide exploration based on real-time observations.

Result: DB-Nav shows superior performance on ObjectNav benchmarks with higher success rates and improved efficiency compared to current techniques.

Conclusion: DB-Nav offers an effective, interpretable solution for object navigation, minimizing reliance on complex vision-language models.

Abstract: Object navigation requires an agent to locate a target in an unknown environment through visual observations. Existing methods typically rely on open-vocabulary detectors or vision-language models (VLMs) to answer where to search, but often overlook what not to trust - which semantic cues are unreliable. Open-vocabulary perception is prone to systematic misleading evidence: false positives, outdated static priors, and repeated failed exploration due to lack of embodied verification, which contaminates mapping and decision-making. Such errors are rooted in structured object relations in real-world scenes. To address this, we propose DB-Nav, a framework that reshapes the search space via dual relational biases. It factorizes target-centric relations into an Activation Bias (propagates contextual evidence) and an Inhibition Bias (suppresses unreliable regions via perceptual confusion and action-level falsification). These biases are unified into a Relational Activation-Inhibition Exploration Graph that modulates frontier exploration values using online observations and failed accesses. Experiments on ObjectNav benchmarks show that DB-Nav significantly outperforms existing methods in success rate (SR) and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL), offering a lightweight, interpretable, and robust navigation framework without costly online VLM reasoning.

</details>


### [205] [HiMem-WAM: Hierarchical Memory-Gated World Action Models for Robotic Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10363)
*Xiaoquan Sun,Ruijian Zhang,Chen Cao,Yihan Sun,Jiahui Chen,Zetian Xu,Bo Chen,Haijier Chen,Zhen Yang,Jiarun Zhu,Yijun Hong,JingZhe Xu,Jingrui Pang,Mingqi Yuan,Jiayu Chen*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: HiMem-WAM, a new Hierarchical Memory-Gated World Action Model, enhances task-relevant memory in long-horizon robotic manipulation, showcasing improved robustness and effectiveness in handling complex tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite advancements in World Action Models (WAMs) for action-relevant visual dynamics, there is a persistent challenge with long-horizon task memory in robotic manipulation.

Method: HiMem-WAM incorporates a hierarchical action framework with motion-centric latent actions, high-level skill latents, and boundary-triggered memory updates for enhanced task memory and causal inference.

Result: HiMem-WAM outperforms existing models in robustness during implementation and significantly aids long-term manipulation tasks, as validated through evaluations on various benchmarks including LIBERO and real-world scenarios.

Conclusion: The integration of hierarchical latents and a memory module in HiMem-WAM results in improved handling of memory-dependent tasks, thereby advancing the capabilities of robotic systems in complex environments.

Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a new powerful paradigm for embodied intelligence, learning action-relevant visual dynamics that significantly enhance generalization and robustness. However, existing WAMs still struggle with task-relevant memory in long-horizon robotic manipulation. To address this, we present HiMem-WAM, a Hierarchical Memory-Gated WAM that integrates motion-centric latent actions, high-level skill latents, and boundary-triggered memory updates. Specifically, we develop a hierarchical latent action framework that jointly learns low-level motion and high-level skill latents, providing structured temporal abstraction. Meanwhile, a boundary-aware memory gate writes compact task states at predicted skill transitions, enabling causal inference without test-time generation of future video or optical flow estimation. Evaluated on LIBERO, LIBERO-PLUS, RMBench and real-world tasks, HiMem-WAM shows that hierarchical latents improve robustness under deployment perturbations, and the memory module substantially benefits memory-dependent long-horizon manipulation.

</details>


### [206] [A Practical Recipe Towards Improving Sim-and-Real Correlation for VLA Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10366)
*Shuo Wang,Hanyuan Xu,Yingdong Hu,Fanqi Lin,Yang Gao*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: This work investigates the correlation between simulation and real-world evaluations of vision-language-action (VLA) policies to enhance the effectiveness of simulation in robot evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation behind this study is to address the gap in reliability of simulation as proxies for real-world evaluations of VLA policies despite advancements in realism and diversity of simulation benchmarks.

Method: A systematic study is conducted involving multiple simulation platforms, VLA policies, tasks, and perturbation factors to measure sim-and-real correlations in policy ranking, performance, and failure patterns.

Result: The analysis reveals limitations of existing simulators and identifies the types of simulation signals that align better with real-world outcomes, alongside guidance for effective use of simulation in policy development.

Conclusion: The work culminates in a unified framework that enhances the understanding and application of simulations in VLA policy refinement, aimed at aiding both simulator developers and practitioners.

Abstract: Simulation has become an essential tool for evaluating and improving vision-language-action (VLA) policies, offering scalable, reproducible, and controllable alternatives to costly real-world robot evaluation. Recent simulation benchmarks have made substantial progress on realism and diversity, yet these platforms have not been widely adopted as reliable proxies for real-world policy evaluation. In this work, we investigate this issue through the lens of sim-and-real correlation. We conduct a systematic study across multiple simulation platforms, VLA policies, tasks, and perturbation factors, measuring whether simulated evaluation preserves real-world conclusions in terms of policy ranking consistency, performance correlation, and perturbation-wise failure patterns. This analysis allows us to characterize the limitations of existing simulators and identify what kinds of simulation signals are more aligned with real-world deployment. We further examine how users should exploit simulation for policy improvement, including when simulator-based finetuning is beneficial and how the amount of post-training data affects sim-and-real alignment. Overall, our work provides a unified framework for measuring, interpreting, and improving the usefulness of simulation for VLA policies, offering guidance both for simulator designers and for practitioners who use simulation as part of the policy development pipeline.

</details>


### [207] [Test-time Adversarial Takeover: A Real-time Hijacking Interface against Robotic Diffusion Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10371)
*Zi Yin,Peilin Chai,Siyuan Huang,Zhanhao Hu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: This paper presents a novel adversarial attack, Test-time Adversarial Takeover (TAKO), targeting diffusion-based action generation in embodied AI by exploiting visual conditioning vulnerabilities to gain control over robotic policies for malicious purposes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to highlight vulnerabilities in visuomotor policies that can be exploited through adversarial manipulation, specifically focusing on the severe threat of remotely piloting robots via adaptive visual perturbations.

Method: TAKO uses differentiable diffusion inference to create a vocabulary of universal patches, which are switched in real time during the task to override the robot's intended trajectories based on visual input.

Result: The approach allows human operators to control the robot with 100% success across various tasks and configurations, demonstrating effectiveness and exposing severe weaknesses in existing systems.

Conclusion: The study reveals that standard adversarial defenses, like target-policy matching, are inadequate, emphasizing the need for improved robustness in visuomotor control policies against sophisticated adversarial attacks.

Abstract: Diffusion-based action generation has become a foundational component of embodied AI, but its reliance on visual conditioning leaves deployed visuomotor policies vulnerable to adversarial manipulation. Most prior attacks focus on disruption: they perturb the observation stream to reduce task success or induce erratic behavior. We study a stronger threat, Test-time Adversarial Takeover (TAKO), in which an attacker obtains a real-time steering interface over a frozen robot policy and turns it into a remotely piloted instrument. TAKO learns a small vocabulary of reusable universal patches through differentiable diffusion inference; at test time, the attacker switches among these patches in the camera stream to compose attacker-chosen trajectories. This works because the perturbation acts on the visual conditioning pathway, where the induced bias can persist through iterative generative inference. We further show that the natural targeted baseline, target-policy matching, fails because the victim policy cannot reliably supervise itself on out-of-distribution target shifts. Across four tasks (2D manipulation, simulated aerial delivery, simulated ground navigation, and physical-world ground navigation), two visual encoders (ResNet-18 and EfficientNet-B0 + Transformer), and three generative inference families (DDPM, DDIM, and flow matching), human operators achieve 100\% takeover success on attacker-defined objectives in every evaluated setting. The project page is available at https://tako-attack.github.io.

</details>


### [208] [UMI-Bench 1.0: An Open and Reproducible Real-World Benchmark for Tabletop Robotic Manipulation with UMI Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10382)
*Shi Jin,Yuntian Wang,Yuhui Duan,Di Wu,Gaoqi Dong,Xiaohang Liu,Xiaotong Li,Hongfei Jia,Zehao Zhang,Tianyu Wang,Zhongjie Jia,Yuanqi Yao,Chenjia Bai,Zhaxizhuoma,Siao Liu,Nieqing Cao,Jin Wang,Chao Yu,Yan Ding*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Introduction of UMI-Bench 1.0, a benchmark for evaluating UMI-style manipulation policies in real robot scenarios, ensuring standardized and reproducible assessments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate the reliability of learned manipulation policies outside of controlled demonstrations, particularly for UMI-style policies reliant on multiple factors.

Method: Development of UMI-Bench 1.0 which standardizes data collection, execution, and analysis for evaluating UMI-based manipulation policies in real-world settings.

Result: UMI-Bench is the first benchmark focused on the real-world evaluation of UMI-style manipulation, improving reproducibility and auditability in testing policies.

Conclusion: UMI-Bench serves as a practical testbed to assess how well UMI-trained policies can generalize to real physical manipulation tasks.

Abstract: Real-robot evaluation is essential for understanding whether learned manipulation policies can operate reliably outside curated demonstrations. This need is particularly pressing for Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI)-style policies, whose performance depends on the coupling between wrist-view observations, action representation, data collection, and physical deployment. Existing real-world benchmarks have made important progress, but they are not designed around this UMI data-to-deployment setting. We present UMI-Bench 1.0, a local-first real-robot benchmark for standardized evaluation of UMI-style manipulation policies. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first benchmark dedicated to real-world evaluation of UMI-based manipulation models. UMI-Bench aligns data collection, scene reset, policy execution, result logging, and task-factor analysis within a unified protocol. By making the full evaluation process reproducible and auditable, UMI-Bench provides a practical testbed for measuring how UMI-trained policies generalize to real physical manipulation.

</details>


### [209] [Information-Preserving Continuous Occupancy Mapping with Variance-Weighted Submap Joining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10442)
*Zhuhua Bai,Yingyu Wang,Liang Zhao,Shoudong Huang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: This paper introduces a continuous probabilistic framework for submap joining in SLAM, improving pose accuracy and map consistency over traditional methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the issues of trajectory drift and computational costs in large-scale SLAM, particularly due to limitations in discrete grid approaches to submap joining.

Method: The proposed method optimizes submap poses and a global occupancy field in the latent log-odds space, using a sparse Bayesian formulation to convert occupancy data into log-odds tuples that capture posterior information.

Result: The framework achieves higher pose accuracy and improved global consistency compared to existing grid-based methods, while also offering compact map representations and well-calibrated uncertainty estimates.

Conclusion: In summary, the proposed continuous probabilistic submap joining framework provides significant advancements in SLAM performance by optimizing occupancy mappings and submap poses more effectively than traditional techniques.

Abstract: Large-scale SLAM remains challenging due to accumulated trajectory drift and the increasing computational cost of maintaining global consistency. Submap joining alleviates these issues by constructing locally consistent submaps and subsequently fusing them into a global map. However, existing occupancy-based submap joining methods operate on discrete grids, resulting in non-smooth gradients during optimization and neglecting the uncertainty associated with occupancy estimates. We propose the first continuous probabilistic submap joining framework that jointly optimizes submap poses and a global occupancy field in the latent log-odds space. The framework employs an information-preserving sparse Bayesian formulation that compresses raw occupancy observations into sufficient-statistic log-odds tuples while retaining the posterior information of the original observations. This yields closed-form predictive mean and variance estimates for occupancy mapping, which directly enable a submap joining formulation with analytical Jacobians, leading to more accurate submap joining and yielding a closed-form optimal global map upon pose convergence. Experiments on both simulated and large-scale real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves higher pose accuracy and improved global consistency than state-of-the-art grid-based submap joining approaches, while producing more compact map representations and better-calibrated uncertainty estimates than existing continuous occupancy mapping methods.

</details>


### [210] [GuideWalk: Learning Unified Autonomous Navigation and Locomotion for Humanoid Robots across Versatile Terrains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10449)
*Haoxuan Han,Chen Chen,Linao Gong,Xin Yang,Hao Hu,Junhong Guo,Zhicheng He,Yao Su,Fenghua He*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: GuideWalk is a robust framework for humanoid navigation that combines traversability-aware guidance with terrain-adaptive locomotion through a novel teacher distillation approach.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve humanoid robots' navigation capabilities on diverse terrains by integrating obstacle avoidance with motion viability.

Method: An end-to-end framework featuring a navigation module for explicit velocity guidance and a composite teacher distillation scheme refined by reinforcement learning and behavior cloning.

Result: GuideWalk successfully enables stable navigation and effective locomotion for humanoids across varying environments.

Conclusion: The framework demonstrates significant improvements in navigating complex terrains while maintaining locomotion stability.

Abstract: Humanoid robots have achieved strong locomotion capabilities, but reliable navigation on versatile terrains remains challenging because obstacle avoidance must be coordinated with dynamically feasible motion. In this work, we present GuideWalk, a unified end-to-end framework that integrates traversability-aware navigation guidance with terrain-adaptive locomotion teacher for humanoid navigation. Specifically, we introduce a navigation module that provides explicit velocity guidance, decoupling obstacle avoidance from terrain conditions to enable robust planning across diverse environments. We propose a composite teacher distillation scheme, where goal-directed commands and dynamically consistent actions are aggregated and distilled into a single policy. To further improve robustness, the distilled policy is refined with reinforcement learning and an auxiliary behavior cloning objective, which promotes exploration while preserving desirable teacher behaviors. Experiments demonstrate that GuideWalk achieves stable and effective navigation while maintaining stable humanoid locomotion.

</details>


### [211] [Act on What You See: Unlocking Safe Social Navigation in Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10495)
*Qingzi Wang,Xiyang Wu,Guangyao Shi,Dianwei Chen,Xianfeng Yang,Dinesh Manocha*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A study introducing SALSA, an annotation-free framework that enhances the social navigation capabilities of robots by aligning existing internal representations with actions, resulting in significant reductions in near-collisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for robots to safely navigate social environments by distinguishing people from obstacles and reacting appropriately to avoid danger.

Method: A two-stage framework: 1) social behavioral alignment to connect social features to actions using counterfactual training, and 2) temporal safety alignment to provide risk supervision for collision avoidance.

Result: An 86.4% reduction in near-collisions and an increase in social counterfactual accuracy from 53% to 93% on SCAND and in real-world applications.

Conclusion: Pretrained VLA policies can achieve safer navigation through improved alignment of latent representations with the necessary actions.

Abstract: Safe social navigation requires robots to distinguish people from ordinary obstacles and to react before danger becomes imminent.
